q: A 3 month old purebred dog presents with ataxia, intention tremors, swaying, and a broad-based stance. The signs were absent at birth and emerged at about 6 weeks. Other than this, the dog is bright and otherwise well. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Cerebellar abiotrophy
Acquired vestibular disease
Lysosomal storage disease in advanced phase
Intracranial primary neoplasia
e: Cerebellar abiotrophy is heritable, dogs are normal at birth, and signs appear at 2 to 9 weeks with onset before 4 months. Lysosomal storage disease shows progressive signs within the first year and is rare; intracranial neoplasia is a senior-onset differential.

q: Which structural and functional changes have been documented in canine cognitive dysfunction syndrome?
o: Diffuse cerebellar atrophy with sparing of the forebrain
Selective hippocampal hypertrophy and dopamine receptor proliferation
Reduced frontal volume, increased ventricles, meningeal calcification, beta-amyloid accumulation, MAOB upregulation, oxidative damage
Acute infarction of the basal ganglia
e: Canine CCDS resembles Alzheimer's disease: frontal atrophy, ventricular enlargement, beta-amyloid, MAOB upregulation, lipofuscin and apoptotic bodies, neuronal loss, and oxidative damage.

q: An 8 year old owner-relinquished dog presents with insidious onset of dementia, head pressing, and altered habits. The most likely diagnosis is:
o: Acute traumatic brain injury
Lysosomal storage disease
Cerebellar abiotrophy
Primary intracranial neoplasia (e.g. meningioma)
e: Primary intracranial tumours (meningioma, astrocytoma) usually occur in dogs over 7 years and cause insidious, slowly progressive signs including dementia, head pressing, and altered habits. Secondary (metastatic) tumours cause acute signs.

q: Selegiline is being considered for a senior dog with cognitive dysfunction. Which combination is STRICTLY contraindicated due to fatal serotonin toxicity risk?
o: Concurrent use with phenobarbital
Concurrent use with SSRIs or TCAs
Concurrent use with calcium-channel blockers
Concurrent use with omeprazole
e: Selegiline (a MAOB inhibitor) combined with SSRIs or TCAs can produce fatal serotonin syndrome. Tramadol, SAMe, tryptophan, and buspirone also add serotonergic risk.

q: Which statement best defines a stereotypy in the veterinary behavioural sense?
o: An abnormal, invariant, repetition of a motor pattern that serves no apparent function
A normal exploratory behaviour displayed in a novel environment
A learned response shaped by positive reinforcement
A breed-specific predatory motor pattern displayed during play
e: A stereotypy is an abnormal, invariant repetition of a motor pattern with no apparent function; it commonly arises from conflict, frustration, or confinement-related stress.

q: At what age do compulsive disorders most commonly arise in dogs and cats?
o: Within the first 2 weeks of life
Only in geriatric patients over 12 years
Prepubertal at 3 to 6 months, or before social maturity at 12 to 36 months
Exclusively during late adolescence between 7 and 8 months
e: Compulsive disorders most commonly arise in the prepubertal period (3 to 6 months), before social maturity (12 to 36 months), or after a recognisable period of change or distress.

q: Among the TCAs, which is the MOST SELECTIVE serotonin reuptake inhibitor and the standard TCA choice for ALD, spinning, tail chasing, and feline psychogenic alopecia?
o: Amitriptyline
Nortriptyline
Doxepin
Clomipramine
e: Clomipramine is the most selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitor of all TCAs and is the standard for compulsive disorders. Other TCAs have less SSRI effect and are less effective for these conditions.

q: An NMDA receptor antagonist is being trialled for a refractory compulsive disorder. What efficacy and time course should you discuss with the owner?
o: Always 100% effective within 24 hours
About 64% effective within 2 weeks, with possible synergy when combined with fluoxetine
About 10% effective only after 6 months of continuous use
Effective only when combined with opiate agonists
e: Memantine and similar NMDA antagonists block glutamate-sensitive NMDA receptors. The notes report about 64% effective within 2 weeks of treatment, with possible synergy with fluoxetine.

q: A compulsive disorder responds well to clomipramine over 6 weeks. The owner asks how long to continue the medication. Which is the correct recommendation?
o: Continue for at least 6 months, often lifelong; if tapering, do so very gradually over several months
Stop immediately once the behaviour resolves
Continue for exactly 2 weeks beyond resolution then stop
Switch to selegiline as soon as improvement is documented
e: If a compulsive disorder improves on medication, the drug should be continued for AT LEAST 6 months, often lifelong. Premature taper risks immediate relapse.

q: A cat presents with episodic rippling of the dorsal skin, spasms of the epaxial muscles inducible by rubbing the back, and self-directed tail biting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Cerebellar abiotrophy
Acute intervertebral disc herniation
Feline hyperesthesia syndrome
Hyperthyroid storm
e: The hallmark of feline hyperesthesia syndrome is rippling or twitching of the thoracolumbar skin and spasm of the epaxial muscles, often inducible by rubbing the back and impossible to interrupt; tail and flank self-trauma is common.

q: A dog displays vocalisation, destructiveness, and housesoiling only when the owner is away from home. Other medical and behavioural causes have been ruled out. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Resource guarding
Predatory aggression
Compulsive disorder
Separation anxiety
e: The classic triad of separation anxiety is vocalisation, destructiveness, and housesoiling that occur ONLY when the owner is absent. If the behaviour also occurs when the family is home, or only randomly rather than consistently on departure, consider other differentials.

q: Which statement best reflects the comparative effectiveness of antidepressants for separation anxiety in dogs?
o: Amitriptyline worked in about 95% of cases compared with fluoxetine at about 20%
Amitriptyline worked in about 56% of cases compared with fluoxetine or clomipramine at about 75%
All antidepressants are equally effective at about 50%
Selegiline is first line and works in 100% of cases
e: The notes report amitriptyline effective in about 56% of cases, while fluoxetine or clomipramine were effective in about 75% of cases for separation anxiety.

q: Which four pillars should anchor the management of separation anxiety?
o: Shape independence; reduce departure and homecoming anxiety; decouple departure cues; anxiety reduction through structure and predictability
Use harsh punishment; restrict water; restrain in a small crate; confront the dog
Feed only on departure; allow constant attention; never crate; use force-based correction
Switch homes weekly; play loud music continuously; ignore all distress; never train
e: The four pillars are: shape independence and remove rewards for attention seeking; reduce departure and homecoming anxiety; decouple departure cues from actual departures via mock departures with a unique non-departure cue; reduce overall anxiety with structure and predictability.

q: An owner reports their dog digs persistently in the yard. Which differential is LEAST likely to drive digging in this clinical setting?
o: Predatory drive directed at burrowing rodents
Separation anxiety and escape attempts
Hypothyroidism
Noise-phobia escape attempts
e: Digging is an innate trait in many breeds, especially terriers, and is most commonly driven by predatory exploration of prey odours, escape from separation anxiety or noise phobia, or insufficient stimulation. Hypothyroidism is not described as a digging driver in the notes.

q: A cat is observed approaching a vertical wall, standing with tail erect, treading the rear legs, and spraying a stream of urine. This posture and behaviour are diagnostic of:
o: Inappropriate toileting due to substrate aversion
A medical urinary tract disorder
Cognitive dysfunction-related housesoiling
Urine marking
e: Marking posture is VERTICAL surface, standing with TAIL ERECT, treading with the rear legs, and spraying. Inappropriate toileting is typically horizontal squat onto a horizontal surface.

q: An adult intact male cat sprays urine indoors. What proportional reduction in spraying can the owner expect after castration, and how does this compare with the effect of spaying in females who spray?
o: Castration reduces spraying in about 50% of males; spaying has no effect in females
Castration reduces spraying in about 90% of males; spaying reduces spraying in about 95% of females
Castration eliminates spraying in 100% of males; spaying eliminates it in 100% of females
Surgery has no proven effect on spraying behaviour
e: Castration reduces spraying in about 90% of males and spaying in about 95% of females.

q: What is the recommended minimum litterbox-to-cat ratio in a multi-cat household?
o: 1 box per cat plus 1 (n + 1)
1 box per 5 cats
2 boxes per cat regardless of household size
No specific ratio is recommended
e: At least 1 box per cat plus 1, with bigger and more boxes generally better.

q: What size and cleaning routine for litterboxes are recommended in the notes?
o: At least 0.5 times the cat's length, scooped weekly, cleaned monthly with bleach
Any commercial size, scooped twice weekly, cleaned with concentrated quaternary ammonium
At least 1.5 times the cat's length, scooped 1 to 2 times daily, cleaned and changed weekly with hot water, avoiding strong disinfectants
No size or cleaning routine recommendations exist in the literature
e: The notes recommend boxes at least 1.5 times the cat's length, scooped 1 to 2 times daily, cleaned and changed weekly with hot water, avoiding strong disinfectants.

q: A young female puppy urinates a small amount whenever excited or when a visitor leans down to greet her. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Verbally correct the puppy each time it urinates so it learns not to do it
Withhold water for several hours before any greeting
Confine the puppy permanently to prevent any greetings
Greet calmly and predictably, ignore the puppy until calm, reinforce only behaviours incompatible with submission or excitement, do not punish; the problem usually improves with age
e: Submissive or excitement urination requires calm greetings, ignoring until calm, response substitution to incompatible behaviours, and NO punishment, since punishment makes it worse. The problem typically improves with age.

q: Which of the following canine aggression types is described in the literature as the MOST mis-diagnosed and OVER-diagnosed?
o: Maternal aggression
Dominance-related aggression
Predatory aggression
Pain-induced aggression
e: Dominance-related aggression is the most mis-diagnosed type. The diagnosis requires confident temperament, assertive signalling, AND aggression toward family members in the ABSENCE of fear. Most owner-directed aggression is actually conflict-related or resource guarding.

q: At approximately what age does resource-guarding aggression typically begin in dogs?
o: About 16 weeks of age
About 2 to 3 weeks of age
Only in geriatric dogs
Exclusively at full sexual maturity at 24 months
e: Resource-guarding age of onset is about 16 weeks. Adult-onset cases can occur in dogs on reducing diets or appetite-stimulating drugs or with appetite-increasing medical conditions like hyperadrenocorticism.

q: Which combination of signs is most consistent with FEAR-RELATED canine aggression rather than offensive aggression?
o: Lean forward, fixed hard eye, raised tail, stiff and frozen body, closed mouth, offensive pucker
Ears forward, tail down but not tucked, prolonged focus on the stimulus
Tail down or tucked, ears back, crouched body, weight shifted away, attempts to escape, piloerection, dilated pupils, tachypnoea
Tail high and fast biased to the right, loose side-to-side wag, open relaxed mouth
e: Fear-related aggression body cluster: tail down or tucked, ears back, crouched body, weight shifted away, escape attempts, plus autonomic signs (piloerection, dilated pupils, tachypnoea, defaecation, urination). Posturing can look offensive when behind a barrier or at a distance.

q: A dog stalks, chases, bites, and shakes a small moving stimulus with minimal prior threat display. This pattern is characteristic of which aggression type?
o: Conflict-related aggression
Pain-induced aggression
Maternal aggression
Predatory aggression
e: Predatory aggression is normal hunting behaviour: stalking, chasing, catching, biting, killing, and sometimes eating, triggered by movement, with little vocal or postural threat. Targets are usually smaller and moving.

q: Which demographic of intraspecific household aggression is over-represented in dogs?
o: Opposite-sex pairs, especially intact males
Same-sex pairs, especially females, with spayed females over-represented
Only multi-breed households with three or more dogs
Exclusively senior dogs over 12 years
e: Most intraspecific household aggression involves same-sex pairs, most often FEMALES; SPAYED FEMALES are over-represented. Younger dogs, new arrivals, and rehomed dogs are most likely to initiate.

q: At what age does feline play aggression typically peak before waning with maturity?
o: About 9 to 12 months
About 1 to 2 weeks
About 5 to 7 years
About 14 to 18 years
e: Feline play aggression usually peaks at 9 to 12 months and wanes as the cat grows into adulthood. Risk is higher in solo-housed cats, hand-raised kittens, and cats encouraged to play with hands and feet.

q: A cat solicits petting then suddenly bites after the owner strokes the lower back for an extended period. This is the SECOND most frequent referral form of feline aggression. What is the diagnosis?
o: Predatory play aggression
Pathophysiological aggression
Petted-induced aggression
Maternal aggression
e: Petted-induced aggression is the second most frequent referred form. The cat may seem to enjoy attention, then has a limited threshold for stroking, classically over the lower back, after which it bites.

q: Which is the correct distinction between Feliway and Felifriend?
o: Feliway and Felifriend are identical products with different brand names
Feliway is for dogs; Felifriend is for cats
Felifriend is a controlled antiviral, Feliway is a behaviour drug

Feliway uses the facial pheromone for environmental marking to reduce stress; Felifriend uses the allomarking pheromone to promote cat-to-cat familiarisation, best applied on the unfamiliar person or animal before introduction
e: Feliway is the facial pheromone associated with environmental marking, reducing stress and anxiety. Felifriend is the allomarking pheromone, applied on the unfamiliar person or animal BEFORE introduction to promote cat-to-cat familiarisation.

q: When evaluating a dog from a fighting environment for inter-dog aggression, what is the correct order and method of stimulus-dog introduction?
o: Always begin with a SAME-SEX stimulus dog off-leash with no barrier to allow natural assessment
Begin with an OPPOSITE-SEX, unrelated stimulus dog through a chain-link fence barrier with both dogs on leashes, progressing to same-sex if neutral
Never use a stimulus dog; rely solely on owner history
Use only a fake dog and skip live stimulus dogs entirely
e: Fighting dogs often react more favourably to opposite-sex dogs first; same-sex introduction follows. Initial contact is through a chain-link fence with both on leashes, since ears, paws, tails, and lips can still be bitten through the fence. Stimulus dogs should be completely unrelated to the case.

q: Which set of behaviours in the fake-dog test is most consistent with TRUE inter-dog aggression that makes a dog unsafe around other animals and is reported to point to euthanasia as the recommended outcome with no current evidence for behavioural modification?
o: Lunging, intense focus, slow stalking, growling, excited barking or silent attack with no hesitation, full-mouthed bite-and-shake
Approaching the fake dog with a relaxed wag and play bow
Sniffing the fake dog briefly then walking away
Lying down at a distance and ignoring the fake dog
e: True aggression toward the fake dog includes lunging, intense focus, slow stalking, growling and snapping, excited or silent barking, attack with no hesitation or once the fake dog rears or falls, and full-mouthed bites with hold and shake. The notes record euthanasia as the recommended outcome for these dogs.

q: What proportion of former puppy-mill breeding dogs continue to exhibit behaviour problems (fear, housesoiling, touch sensitivity, compulsive behaviour, compromised quality of life) after rehoming?
o: About 5%
Less than 1%
About 83%
Exactly 50%
e: The notes record that approximately 83% of former puppy-mill breeding dogs still exhibit behaviour problems in the home after rehoming, with a compromised quality of life.
